Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, s. 15(1)
.
Section 28(1) of R.R.O. 1980, Reg. 262, as revised, enacted under the Education Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 129, provides that "a public school shall be opened or closed each school day with religious exercises consisting of the reading of the Scriptures or other suitable readings and repeating of the Lord's Prayer or other suitable prayers". On an application, inter alia, for a declaration that s. 28(1) is of no force or effect because it violates
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, held, Reid J. dissenting, the application should be dismissed.
Per O'Leary J.: Section 28(1) of R.R.O. 1980, Reg. 262 does not require anyone to participate in or be present at religious exercises. There was no evidence that the pressure to participate in the religious exercises created by s. 28(1) was substantial. The type of coercion complained of was pressure to conform rather than face the embarrassment of disclosing that a different belief was held. This does not constitute coercion to such an extent as to infringe the right of freedom of conscience and religion under
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
. Even if it could be said that the pressure to participate in religious exercises created by s. 28(1) was an infringement of freedom of conscience and religion, it was such an infringement as could be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society and so constituted a reasonable limit on such freedom under
s. 1
of the Charter. Schools have an obligation to teach morality. While some may argue that morality can be taught without associating it with God, few would deny that in the minds of most persons morality and religion are intertwined and that to associate God and morality is an effective way of teaching morality. That some pupils may feel pressure to participate in religious exercises to avoid the embarrassment of disclosing a different belief is, at most, a minor infringement of their freedom of conscience and religion and must not be allowed to stand in the way of the obligation of the schools to teach morality in the most effective and least offensive way they know how, namely, by holding religious exercises.
Per O'Leary J., Anderson J. concurring: Section 28(1) does not discriminate against non-Christians contrary to
s. 15(1)
of the
Charter
. The subsection merely provides that the religious exercises consist of the reading of the Scriptures or other suitable readings, and the repeating of the Lord's Prayer or other suitable prayers. Accepting that the Scriptures and Lord's Prayer are solely Christian forms of devotion, the "other suitable readings" or "other suitable prayers" do not have to be. The religious exercises required by s. 28(1) do not have to be Christian and can be adapted by the school board and teachers as suits the particular make-up of any classroom. Section 28(1) does not require or encourage religious discrimination so far as believers are concerned. Non-believers may argue that the mere holding of religious exercises gives believers an opportunity to reinforce their beliefs that is not afforded non-believers. If this be religious discrimination then it constitutes a reasonable limit or infringement under s. 1 of the Charter of the right given by
s. 15(1)
. Where a country is founded on the principle of the supremacy of God there is no obligation on the schools to spend the same effort reinforcing the belief of non-believers that God does not exist as in teaching believers about the nature of God.
Per Anderson J.: Section 28(1) of R.R.O. 1980, Reg. 262 does not, either in purpose or effect, compel, coerce or constrain anyone and hence does not violate
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
. It contains, in s. 28(10), a complete and unconditional provision that no pupil shall be required to take part in any religious exercise. It is argued that the right to abstain from the exercises or be absent from them, far from saving the regulation in fact condemns it; that the mere provision of this right implies that the exercises may be offensive to some, and that the need to have recourse to the right of abstention or absence is in itself constraint, compulsion or coercion, or at least a major inducement. Thus baldly stated, the argument offends logic and common sense. It is tantamount to saying that a right to refuse is a compulsion to accept. Choice is of the essence of freedom and the decision as to what choice is appropriate is often difficult. The difficulty is part of the price of freedom.
Per Reid J. dissenting: Section 28(1) is mandatory. A law that requires the performance of religious exercises is a restriction on freedom of religion. That is so even if the exercise be of a person's own religion. Section 28(10) provides for an election. If, standing together, s-ss. (1) and (10) offered a truly free choice, there would be no restriction, and nothing contrary to the
Charter
. But there is a difference between imposing a rule and providing for exceptions, on the one hand, and providing truly alternative choices on the other. Had the object been to provide real freedom of choice, it could easily have been achieved. All that was required was to provide that there would be a time during the day when those who wished could take part in religious exercises and those who did not, need not. While such a provision might possibly be effected in some schools so as to make those who wished not to participate feel "different" or "left out" in the hope that they would join the participating group, the provision on its face would not be objectionable under the Charter. On its face, however, the regulation discloses a purpose contrary to the Charter: a purpose to interfere with religious freedom.
As to the regulation's effect, there was evidence that some parents and students felt compelled to refrain from asserting their right to elect. This did not stem from fear of penal sanctions but penal sanctions are not necessary to the existence of compulsion. Compulsion may take many forms. It may be that a control or limitation indirectly imposed is not readily appreciable to those who are not affected by it. It may be difficult for members of a majoritarian religious group to appreciate the feelings of members of minority religions. It may be difficult for religious people to appreciate the feelings of agnostics and atheists. Nevertheless those feelings exist. The effect of s. 28 is contrary to both
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the
Charter
.
Section 28 cannot be saved by
s. 1
of the
Charter
. It is not a reasonable limitation on religious freedom. No governmental concern has been demonstrated so pressing as to justify the obvious interference with religious freedom sought by and caused by the regulation. In addition, s. 1 was not intended to be applied so as to justify an interference with the religious freedom of some but not of others. That would make the Charter contradict itself. If any interference may be justified by reason of s. 1, it must be an interference not with the right of some to religious freedom, but with the right of all.

O'LEARY J.:-- This is an application pursuant to
s. 24(1)
of
the
Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms
, Constitution Act,
1982 (the "Charter"), for judicial review of the jurisdiction
of the Sudbury Board of Education (the "Board") to hold
religious exercises in its schools and to require the
recitation of the Lord's Prayer in those exercises, and for a
declaration that s. 28(1) of R.R.O. 1980, Reg. 262 under the
Education Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 129, is of no force and effect
because it violates the said Charter and the Ontario Human
Rights Code, 1981 (Ont.), c. 53. Regulation 262 (as revised by
O. Reg. 617/81) reads in part:

RELIGIOUS EXERCISES AND RELIGIOUS
EDUCATION IN THE PUBLIC SCHOOLS

28(1) A public school shall be opened or closed each school
day with religious exercises consisting of the reading of the
Scriptures or other suitable readings and the repeating of
the Lord's Prayer or other suitable prayers.

(2) The readings and prayers that form part of the
religious exercises referred to in subsection (1) shall be
chosen from a list of selections approved for such purpose by
the board that operates the school where the board approves
such a list and, where the board does not approve such a
list, the principal of the school shall select the readings
and prayers after notifying the board of the principal's
intention to do so, but this selection is subject to revision
by the board at any time.

(3) The religious exercises under subsection (1) may
include the singing of one or more hymns.

. . . . .

(10) No pupil shall be required to take part in any
religious exercises ... where a parent of the pupil, or the
pupil where the pupil is an adult, applies to the principal
of the school that the pupil attends for exemption of the
pupil therefrom.

(11) In public schools without suitable waiting rooms or
other similar accommodation, if the parent of a pupil or,
where the pupil is an adult, the pupil applies to the
principal of the school for the exemption of the pupil from
attendance while religious exercises are being held ... such
request shall be granted.

(12) Where a parent of a pupil, or the pupil where the
pupil is an adult, objects to the pupil's taking part in
religious exercises ... but requests that the pupil remain in
the classroom during the time devoted to religious exercises
... the principal of the school that the pupil attends shall
permit the pupil to do so, if the pupil maintains decorous
behaviour.

(13) If, because of the right to be absent from religious
exercises ... any pupil is not present in the classroom
during the periods specified for religious exercises ... the
absence shall not be considered a contravention of the rules
of the school.

The applicants are the parents of children currently
attending or soon to attend public elementary school in
Sudbury.

The applicants Zylberberg and Gregg are of Jewish ancestry
and take pride in their Jewish heritage and culture. Their
spouses are not of Jewish ancestry. The applicant Zylberberg
objects to the religious exercises conducted by the Board on
the basis that the Lord's Prayer, which is repeated during
those exercises, is a prayer accepted only in Christian
practice as a form of supplication and that the Scripture
readings used in the religious exercises are of Christian
origin only. The applicant Gregg states that her family is not
of religious inclination and objects to the religious exercises
on the basis that it is discriminatory of non-believers to
require a religious component to public education. Gregg and
her husband have reached an agreement with the teachers of the
school their 11-year-old daughter attends that their daughter
not participate in the religious exercises but that she remain
in the classroom during the exercises. They believe that it is
not in her interest that she be thus singled out from her
peers.

The applicant Coppel-Park is also of Jewish ancestry, adheres
to the Jewish faith and teachings and attends synagogue with
her five-year-old daughter. Her spouse is not of Jewish
ancestry. She objects to the recitation of the Lord's Prayer or
other prayers in the schools on the basis that such practice
discriminates both against non-Christians and non-believers and
contravenes her daughter's right to freedom of religion.

The applicant Wyers is of Christian ancestry but practises no
faith. His wife is also of Christian ancestry and although not
strictly observant does practise her faith. Their sons attend
the Catholic Church a few times a year. Wyers and his wife made
a decision not to send their children to the separate school in
order that they might secure a secular and not a religious
education. Wyers objects to the religious exercises, including
the recitation of the Lord's Prayer, on the basis that they
offend his sons' right to freedom of religion and because the
religious exercises being Christian-oriented discriminate
against non-believers and non-Christians. Wyers has not made
his objections known to the Board nor has he asked that his
children be excused from religious exercises because he does
not want them singled out from their peers on the basis of
their beliefs.

The applicant Enver observes the Islamic faith. He objects to
the religious exercises on the basis that they discriminate
against non-Christians and non-believers, but he has not made
his objections known to the Board nor asked that his children
be excused during religious exercises because he does not want
them singled out on the basis of their heritage and belief.

While on the argument of the application before us, counsel
for the applicants asked only that the portion of s. 28(1) of
Reg. 262 reading "and the repeating of the Lord's Prayer or
other suitable prayers" be declared of no force and effect,
counsel for the intervenors asked that all of s. 28(1) be
declared ultra vires.

Accordingly, we must deal with the question of the validity
of s. 28(1) in its entirety and, of course, the propriety of
the actions of the Board in its efforts to implement s. 28(1).

Philip Zylberberg inquired as to the practice of the Board in
regard to religious exercises in its schools. On January 17,
1985, the Board answered, in part, as follows:

... each principal is expected to have opening exercises and
religious exercises that are either conducted by the teacher
in the classroom or over the central public address system.
The exercises are to consist of the playing and/or singing of
the national anthem and the repeating of the Lord's Prayer.
Reading of scripture or bible stories are also to be
included.

Those parents who wish to have their children excluded from
these exercises are allowed to do so.

Should you wish to have further discussion on this matter,
please do not hesitate to contact me.

Mr. Zylberberg answered the Board's letter on March 14, 1985,
as follows:

RE: LORD'S PRAYER AS RELIGIOUS EXERCISES UNDER REGULATION 262

Further to your letter of January 17th, 1985, wherein you
confirm that the Sudbury Board of Education in exercising its
power under Regulation 262 require each principal to hold
opening Lord's Prayer as well as reading of biblical stories,
I wish to voice my objections to this practice.

Given that the date on which the equality provisions of the

Charter of Rights
is to become effective is very soon upon
us, I would request that you review your practices as
outlined in your letter noted above, and bring them into
conformity with the Charter of Rights. The holding of
religious exercises I would suggest offends the rights
guaranteed under the Charter of Rights but certainly the
ruling requires repetition of exclusively Christian
observances offends these fundamental rights and must be
altered.

The practices raise important issues to myself and other
residents and parents in the Sudbury area. I along with
several other concerned residents have already retained and
consulted a solicitor and intend to commence an application
before the Courts once the equality provision under the

Charter of Rights
becomes effective, should you continue with
these practices.

Section 15
of the
Charter
became effective April 17, 1985.

This application was brought by the applicants on April 26,
1985.

The Board has never been requested by the applicants or
anyone else to incorporate into its religious exercises any
prayers or readings which might reflect a religious point of
view or heritage other than the one reflected to this date. The
Board is, however, as appears from the affidavit of James D.
Smith, its director of education, prepared to receive such
requests, meet with concerned parents and vary its practice to
reasonably reflect the multicultural heritage of Canadians.

While the arguments of counsel for the applicants and the
intervenors did not coincide on all points, nothing will be
gained by pointing out the differences in them. In the balance
of these reasons I will refer to all arguments in support of
the application as if made by or for the applicants.

The attack on s. 28(1) of Reg. 262 is based primarily on
ss.
2(a)
and
15(1)
of the
Charter
, which read:

Fundamental Freedoms

2.  Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(a) freedom of conscience and religion;

. . . . .

Equality Rights

15(1)  Every individual is equal before and under the law
and has the right to the equal protection and equal benefit
of the law without discrimination and, in particular, without
discrimination based on race, national or ethnic origin,
colour, religion, sex, age or mental or physical disability.

The complaints of the applicants are:

A. That the requirement that parents or pupils who object to
the pupils' participation in the religious exercises prescribed
by s. 28(1) must ask to be exempted therefrom and that the
pupils must then in fact exempt themselves therefrom, tends to
pressure or coerce the pupils into participating in the
religious exercises, thereby infringing their right to freedom
of conscience and religion.

B. That s. 28(1) contemplates and, as implemented by the Board,
provides Christian religious exercises only, thereby
discriminating against non-Christians contrary to
s. 15(1)
of
the
Charter
.

Before dealing with those complaints, some observations of a
general nature are appropriate.

(
1
) Unlike the Constitution of the United States of America
where the First Amendment provides, "Congress shall make no law
respecting an establishment of religion, or prohibiting the
free exercise thereof ", the
Charter
does not prohibit
governments in Canada from supporting the teaching of religion
or the holding of religious exercises provided of course in
doing so
ss. 2(a)
and
15(1)
of the Charter are not violated.

(
2
) The
Charter
begins with the following words: "Whereas
Canada is founded upon principles that recognize the supremacy
of God and the rule of law".

(
3
)
Section 27
of the
Charter
reads: "This Charter shall be
interpreted in a manner consistent with the preservation and
enhancement of the multicultural heritage of Canadians."

Our Constitution then is based on the existence of a supreme
being -- God, and provides that multiculturalism is to be
allowed to flourish. The recognition in the Constitution of the
existence of God and that our society is multicultural in
nature cannot, of course, excuse a violation of
ss. 2(a)
or

15(1)
of the
Charter
but must be kept in mind when such
violations are alleged.

I turn now to the argument that s. 28(1) of Reg. 262 tends to
coerce pupils into participating in religious exercises and
thereby infringes their right to freedom of conscience and
religion.

I accept that there is or may be pressure on all who are
culturally or religiously different to conform to the ways of
the majority. In particular, I accept that the holding of
religious exercises in the school may constitute some pressure
on students to participate rather than disclose to teachers and
fellow-students that their conscience or religious beliefs
dictate they should not participate.

The applicants submit that the decisions of the Supreme Court
of Canada in R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295,
18 D.L.R. (4th) 321, [1985] 3 W.W.R. 481, and of the Ontario
Court of Appeal in R. v. Videoflicks Ltd. et al. (1984),
1984 CanLII 44 (ON CA)
, 48
O.R. (2d) 395, 14 D.L.R. (4th) 10, 15 C.C.C. (3d) 353, support
their contention that the pressure to participate in religious
exercises I have referred to constitutes an infringement of
their right to freedom of conscience and religion.

Counsel for the applicants pointed to the words of Dickson J.
in Big M, at pp. 336-7 S.C.R., p. 354 D.L.R., p. 518 W.W.R.:

Freedom can primarily be characterized by the absence of
coercion or constraint. If a person is compelled by the state
or the will of another to a course of action or inaction
which he would not otherwise have chosen, he is not acting of
his own volition and he cannot be said to be truly free. One
of the major purposes of the
Charter
is to protect, within
reason, from compulsion or restraint. Coercion includes not
only such blatant forms of compulsion as direct commands to
act or refrain from acting on pain of sanction, coercion
includes indirect forms of control which determine or limit
alternative courses of conduct available to others. Freedom
in a broad sense embraces both the absence of coercion and
constraint, and the right to manifest beliefs and practices.
Freedom means that, subject to such limitations as are
necessary to protect public safety, order, health, or morals
or the fundamental rights and freedoms of others, no one is
to be forced to act in a way contrary to his beliefs or his
conscience.

It must be remembered that these words were written while the
Court was considering a statutory requirement that under pain
of penal consequences Sunday was to be observed as the day of
rest by all no matter what their religious view as to the day
to be so sanctified. Section 28(1) does not, of course, require
anyone to participate in or be present at religious exercises.
In my view, the words of Dickson J. just quoted do not support
the proposition that any amount of pressure, no matter how
slight, tending to influence a pupil to participate in
religious exercises against the dictates of his conscience,
violates
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
.

From the words of Tarnopolsky J.A. in Videoflicks, counsel
for the applicants quoted the following, at p. 423 O.R., pp.
38-9 D.L.R.:

As discussed previously, a law which prohibits certain
practices which are an essential part of one's religion must
be considered an abridgement or infringement of freedom of
religion. This is so even though the impact on religion
occurs, as here, in an indirect sense. While the Act does not
require that one work on one's sabbath, it nevertheless
constitutes a major inducement to do so. For those who
observe a sabbath other than Sunday, being forced to close on
both days of a week-end or, for that matter, any two days in
a week, when one's competitors can remain open for six days,
makes observance of one's sabbath financially onerous.

Tarnopolsky J.A. was dealing with a statute which imposed an
onerous financial burden on one whose sabbath was other than
Sunday. Section 28(1) does not require participation in the
religious exercises or even make it inconvenient for the pupil
at any other time he chooses to pray or direct his thoughts as
his conscience dictates. The words of Tarnopolsky J.A. do not
support the argument that the kind of pressure here exerted on
the pupil to participate constitutes a violation of his freedom
of conscience and religion.

There is no evidence before us to suggest that the pressure
to participate in the religious exercises created by s. 28(1)
is substantial. We have the view of some of the applicants that
it is not in the interest of their children to be singled out
from their peers by exempting themselves out of the religious
exercises. We also have the evidence of Dr. Edward Bassis, a
psychologist, who states in his affidavit:

2.  Where children are in a class where prayer is expected,
but who do not pray, or where prayer does not reflect the
religious beliefs of the family, they will feel themselves
under school pressure to conform, and in conflict as to
whether to submit to the pressure or resist with the
resulting feeling of being different. This may be harmful to
the children when there is pressure to conform, and lack of
understanding in respect of religious differences on the part
of the teachers and children in the major religion.

For the respondent we have the evidence of Donald Robert
Kennedy, Ph.D., a psychologist. I quote from his affidavit:

12.  I do not agree with Dr. Bassis that children from
dissentient families will automatically " ... feel themselves
under school pressure to conform, and in conflict
...". First, the usual instruction to and the normal practice
of teachers in the public school is to minimize the singling
out of any student, especially in a negative manner. Second,
it is common practice in the schools to separate children for
participation in different activities, both within the
individual classroom and outside the classroom within special
groups. This type of alternative activity is sometimes
associated with specific difficulties, sometimes with
enrichment, and sometimes it is simply an alternative for the
student(s) involved. Any such exemption could be construed
negatively by a school staff member or by some children.
However, alternative activities in themselves are the norm
and not at all unusual. Further, specific exemptions, even in
core subjects, are not uncommon. There should be, therefore,
little pressure to conform with respect to any school
activity that has not been assigned to the student involved.
Within individual children there could be some feelings of
conflict around the morning exercises, as there could be in
connection to the many other school activities in which they
do or do not participate. In other children, there should be
no conflict at all.

13.  Although "pressure to conform" and "conflict" should not
be considered as the normal result of exemption from any
school activity, neither should such be characterized as
being "harmful" except in very extreme situations. Nothing in
the Affidavits referred to in paragraph 10, above, suggests
that such extreme circumstances exist. Moderate levels of
"pressure to conform" and "conflict" are part of the
normal developmental process in children, as well as in
adults. In normal children, the most likely result of any
such pressures or conflicts would be to increase the arousal
level and thereby to strengthen the learning process. Under
such conditions, decision making should be reinforced and
self-definition encouraged. In the normal child, with respect
to morning exercises as practised in Ontario public schools,
the expected result would be a strengthening of genuinely
held convictions. In the abnormal child, problems could occur
in relation to this or in relation to any other school or
non-school activity.

Also for the respondent there is the affidavit of Rudolph L.
Philipp who holds a Ph.D. in psychology. He states in part as
follows:

5.  I have reviewed the Affidavits of the Applicants and the
Respondent herein as well as that of Dr. Edward Bassis. Based
upon my own experience as well as my expertise in the field
of child psychology, and bearing in mind the contents of
those affidavits, I believe it is incorrect to say that the
children in question are likely to "suffer harm" due to any
perceived "pressure to conform". While acknowledging that
peer pressure can exist in the school environment, in twenty
years of study and practice in the field of children's mental
health, I have never observed or heard of a case of a child
suffering harm from having to cope with the decision of
whether to participate in or seek exemption from
participating in school prayers.

6.  In my opinion, it is expected and indeed common for
children of whatever faith to have to reconcile differences
between the value and belief systems of their parents and
those with which they come into contact in school and in
society at large. This process is in fact important in the
child's development of his own value and belief system.

In attempting to determine the degree of pressure to conform
created by s. 28(1) and whether such pressure amounts to such
coercion as to infringe
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
, one must bear
in mind that our multicultural heritage is to be preserved and
enhanced. Difference is the very essence of a multicultural
society. Difference is to be worn with pride not hidden. It is
obvious in speech, dress, personal appearance and mannerisms.
Being different from the majority, especially in the large
metropolitan areas of the province, is common-place.

If a child's culture is different to that of the majority,
quite apart from the issue of prayer or religious exercises,
that difference will quickly become apparent to his classmates.
For a child whose culture is different to that of the majority,
the emotional stress of having to disclose his religion is
different to that of the majority, in most cases, must be of
little more consequence than disclosing any of the other
differences that identify the particular culture to which he
belongs.

The child that differs from the majority only in his
religious beliefs might, if s. 28(1) did not exist, hide from
his classmates for some considerable time that his religious
beliefs are different. But it is almost inevitable that sooner
or later, if he associates in a close way with any of his
classmates, it will become known that his religion is different
to the majority. If disclosing a difference in religion is an
embarrassment, it is nevertheless an embarrassment that will
have to be faced throughout life and not just during school
years.

It must be noted that the parent or pupil does not have to
justify in any way his decision not to participate in the
religious exercises. The reason for the decision does not have
to be disclosed. It can be frivolous or even irrelevant.

The applicants' position amounts to this: The very holding of
religious exercises acceptable to most Christians, but not
acceptable to non-Christians, including non-believers, coerces
non-Christians to participate in those religious exercises
since non-Christians may be embarrassed to disclose those
exercises are not acceptable to them. Such coercion the
applicants say violates their right to freedom of conscience
and religion.

The type of coercion complained of, is pressure to conform
rather than face the embarrassment of disclosing that a
different belief is held. If such coercion infringes the
guarantee of freedom of conscience and religion then such
freedom is likewise infringed whenever prayer is said at
functions provided for by statute. For example, a religious
exercise or prayer in Parliament or the Legislature would
infringe the right to freedom of conscience and religion.

In my view, the pressure to conform complained about here
does not constitute coercion to such an extent as to infringe
the right of freedom of conscience and religion.

If contrary to the view I have just expressed it can be said
that the pressure to participate in religious exercises created
by s. 28(1) is an infringement of freedom of conscience and
religion, then, in my view, it is such an infringement as can
be demonstrably justified in a free and democratic society and
so constitutes a reasonable limit on such freedom under
s. 1
of
the
Charter
.

Our schools have an obligation to teach morality. While some
may argue that morality can be taught without associating it
with God, few would deny that in the minds of most persons
morality and religion are intertwined and that to associate God
and morality is an effective way of teaching morality. In my
view, it is as true today as it was in 1950 when these words
appeared in the Hope Commission Report on Education in Ontario
that "religion and morality, though not sectarianism, must have
a central place in any system of education".

That some pupils may feel pressure to participate in
religious exercises to avoid the embarrassment of disclosing a
different belief is, in my view, at most, a minor infringement
of their freedom of conscience and religion and must not be
allowed to stand in the way of the obligation of the schools to
teach morality in the most effective and least offensive way
they know how, namely, by holding religious exercises.

In a country whose constitution is founded on the supremacy
of God, but where regular church attendance is the exception
rather than the rule, care must be taken not to put unnecessary
obstacles in the way of the schools bringing our children into
touch with God by prayer, reflection and meditation as a means
of instilling in them the morality required for social order
and individual happiness.

I now deal with the argument that s. 28(1) discriminates
against non-Christians and so contravenes
s. 15(1)
of the

Charter
.

A literal reading of s. 28(1) does not disclose any
discrimination. The subsection merely provides that the
religious exercises consist of the reading of the Scriptures or
other suitable readings, and the reading of the Lord's Prayer
or other suitable prayers. Accepting that the Scriptures and
Lord's Prayer are solely Christian forms of devotion, the
"other suitable readings" or "other suitable prayers"
certainly do not have to be. The religious exercises required
by s. 28(1) do not then have to be Christian oriented and can
be adapted by the school boards and teachers as suits the
particular makeup of any classroom.

Indeed the latitude that exists under s. 28(1) to devise
religious exercises appropriate to and acceptable to almost all
parents and students has been demonstrated by the efforts in
that regard of the Board of Education for the City of Toronto.
Commencing in 1975, the Toronto Board undertook an extensive
re-examination of the question of religious education and
attempted to devise readings and prayers of a universal nature
in response to the multicultural make-up of the student body in
its schools. In the process the Toronto Board established an
interdenominational committee to recommend suitable readings
and prayers which would reflect the multicultural and
multireligious make-up of its teachers and students.

The result has been the creation of a book of readings and
prayers for use in Toronto schools. The book contains readings
and prayers from the following religious traditions: Baha'i,
Buddhist, Christian, Orthodox, Hindu, Islamic, Jainist, Jewish,
People of Native Ancestry, Secular Humanism, Sikhist and
Zoroastrian. The recommended format for opening religious
exercises as outlined in the book is: (a) O Canada; (b) one or
more selections from the booklet of readings and prayers,
followed by a moment of silent meditation, and (c) suitable
comment by the teacher or principal, if necessary, concerning
the origins of the selections used.

As is stated in the introduction to the book:

It is the intention that suitable readings and prayers from a
variety of traditions be presented to provide focus for the
silent meditation of the students, and to increase student
and staff awareness of the many religious and cultural
traditions of the students in the city's schools. Teachers
and/or the Principal are expected to refer to the
introductory material throughout the Readings and Prayers as
a source of information. This information is presented in a
type different from that of the prayers and readings, and
appears in the pages preceding the prayers and readings of
each tradition. There is a bibliography at the end for
further reference. Teachers are expected to choose material
that is suitable to the age and grade level of their
students.

The following which appears at pp. 11, 12 and 13 of the book
is, I believe, a fair statement as to how the book came into
being and the hopes and expectations of its authors:

The book appeared as much because the parental community of
Toronto wanted it as it did as a response to the law.
Certainly its content and its structure reflect what
representatives of that community believed should be
experienced by students in our schools and what would best
assist teachers and administrators adhere to Regulation 262's
requirements.

Since September 1979, representatives established by
virtually every religious tradition in this city have worked
to compile this book. All inclusions have come from them and
the communities they represented. They have presented those
they believed best represented the teachings, tenets and
hopes of their particular beliefs and yet at no time
undermine those of others found in the book. This caring,
this cooperation, this eager creativity marked the whole
developmental process, and it is in this history of learning
and mutual respect that the committee hopes the inclusions
will be seen and used by those in the schools.

It is evident from those parents and citizens who served on
this committee and from others who spoke to it that religious
contemplation plays a significant role in public education in
this city and that it is seen as an important ingredient in
the public school experience. It is self-evident to all that
Toronto's public schools are multireligious in population,
just as they are multicultural and multiethnic. They have
expressed the belief that exposure to, and contemplation of,
the variety of religious traditions found in each school
community is a positive way of enhancing the understanding
and appreciation of others. They recognized that Toronto
school children come to school each day in support of
different traditions. These traditions are important aspects
of family life and personal identity. All students should
have the opportunity to see their traditions as part of
school life. By providing prayers and readings of these
traditions for use in Opening Exercises it is the committee's
hope that students and teachers will come to learn more about
classmates and students sitting respectively next to, and
before, them.

This view is echoed by the Ecumenical Study Commission
(1984) in its contention that "... a proper understanding
of prayer and Opening Exercises can strengthen rather than
divide the community ...", and again that learning about the
beliefs of others should "... be perceived to be a
strengthening of local religious communities rather than a
threat to them ...".

. . . . .

And finally, understanding and appreciation comes after
information. Exposure to the teachings, convictions and hopes
of others found in the classroom, school and community can
only facilitate the formulation and strengthening of such a
bond. The community representatives who compiled this book
... are deeply interested in public education for they see
public schools as a true reflection of society and an
excellent environment in which to nurture in their own
children and in those of others attitudes and social
relationships that can be carried over into, and benefit, the
society as a whole in which we all live.

. . . . .

Mindful of the importance of information to understanding
and appreciation, the pages beginning each section contain
details about the basic beliefs, doctrine, history and
principal writings of that tradition, along with the most
important holy and festival days over the year.

If this book is used as intended by its authors it is
difficult to see how any pupil could contend that he has been
denied equal opportunity so far as religious education is
concerned. Even non-believers will have difficulty claiming
discrimination for the book contains eight pages contributed by
those who espouse Secular Humanism.

I am satisfied that s. 28(1) does not require or encourage
religious discrimination so far as believers are concerned.

Non-believers, on the other hand, may argue that the mere
holding of religious exercises gives believers an opportunity
to reinforce their beliefs that is not afforded non-believers.
If this is religious discrimination then it constitutes a
reasonable limit or infringement under s. 1 of the Charter of
the right given by
s. 15(1)
.

Where a country is founded on the principle of the supremacy
of God there is no obligation on the schools to spend the same
effort reinforcing the belief of non-believers that God does
not exist as in teaching believers about the nature of God.
Religious exercises for those who wish to take part, in the
absence of any attempt to support the proposition God does not
exist is no more than a reasonable limit, prescribed by law,
reasonably justified in a free and democratic society, on the
right of a non-believer to equal educational benefits.

The applicants submit that in any event the Sudbury Board's
effort at implementing s. 28(1) resulted in religious
discrimination against them. I have already reviewed the
evidence in that regard. It is clear that the religious
exercises directed by the Sudbury Board has generally a
Christian orientation. But no parent or student has suggested
the inclusion of other readings or prayers. The Board has
indicated its willingness to co-operate with the parents to
that end and until an effort has been made by the applicants to
work out with the Board the content of religious exercises that
would be acceptable to them, it would be improper for the Court
to rule on whether or not the Board is discriminating against
the applicants.

The applicants raised some other arguments in support of
their contention that s. 28(1) is invalid. I will state and
then deal in a summary way with these arguments.

That the Education Act does not authorize the enactment of s.
28(1)

Section 50 of the Education Act reads:

50(1) Subject to the regulations, a pupil shall be allowed
to receive such religious instruction as his parent or
guardian desires or, where the pupil is an adult, as he
desires.

(2) No pupil in a public school shall be required to read
or study in or from a religious book, or to join in an
exercise of devotion or religion, objected to by his parent
or guardian, or by the pupil, where he is an adult.

Section 10 reads in part:

10(1) Subject to the approval of the Lieutenant Governor in
Council, the Minister may make regulations in respect of
schools or classes established under this Act, or any
predecessor of this Act, and with respect to all other
schools supported in whole or in part by public money,

. . . . .

18.  governing the provision of religious exercises and
religious education in public and secondary schools and
providing for the exemption of pupils from participating in
such exercises and education and of a teacher from teaching,
and a public school board or a secondary school board from
providing, religious education in any school or class;

In my view, the provisions of the Education Act just quoted
are authority for s. 28(1).

Since the Religious Freedom Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 447, assures
free exercise and enjoyment of religion before any Ontario
statute can interfere with that right it must do so explicitly
and the Education Act does not explicitly authorize prayer in
religious exercises. Section 1 of the Religious Freedom Act
reads:

1. The free exercise and enjoyment of religious profession
and worship, without discrimination or preference, provided
the same be not made an excuse for acts of licentiousness, or
a justification of practices inconsistent with the peace and
safety of the Province, is by the constitution and laws of
this Province assured to all Her Majesty's subjects within
the same.

I have of course already concluded that s. 28(1) does not
infringe the right to freedom of conscience and religion.
Further, I am of the view that the Education Act does
explicitly, or by necessary implication, authorize s. 28(1). In
my view, prayer is so central to religion, that when s. 10(1),
para. 18 of the Education Act authorizes the Minister to make
regulations governing the provision of religious exercises it
has specifically or by necessary implication authorized prayer
as part of those exercises. Prayer is man's effort at communion
with God and a religious exercise is pointless unless it
strives for that communion.

The Human Rights Code, like the Religious Freedom Act, being
a law relating to fundamental values and so of general
application, provides that every person has a right to equal
treatment with respect to services, and so the Education Act
must specifically authorize classroom prayers before s. 28(1)
can be said to be valid. This argument is based on the
assumption that classroom prayer must be discriminatory, a view
I have rejected. In any event, I have already concluded that
the Education Act does by necessary implication authorize
classroom prayer.

In Re Ontario Film & Video Appreciation Society and Ontario
Board of Censors (1983),
1983 CanLII 1923 (ON HCJ)
, 41 O.R. (2d) 583, 147 D.L.R. (3d) 58,
34 C.R. (3d) 73, this Court held that a statutory provision
giving a board the task of censoring films without setting
adequate guidelines as to when it should exercise its power to
censor was invalid on the basis that the power it gave to
censor was not limited or prescribed by law and could not be
saved by the application of
s. 1
of the
Charter
. Section 28(1)
is likewise invalid because it gives school boards the power to
discriminate against non-Christians and has not set a limit on
their right to decide what prayers or readings are to form part
of the religious exercises.

In my view, there is no similarity between the two cases. In
the Ontario Film case the task given the board was to censor.
It was intended that the board would, in the course of its
duties, infringe the freedom of expression guaranteed by
s.
2(a)
of the
Charter
. When the board did censor a film its
conduct in doing so could only be justified if the censoring
was within reasonable limits prescribed by law. The limits
within which the board could censor not having been so
prescribed the statutory provision failed.

Here s. 28(1) does not direct the doing of anything that
would infringe freedom of religion or that is to be carried out
in a way so as to discriminate on the basis of religion. The
fact that some misguided school board or teacher could in
carrying out the direction to hold religious exercises infringe
a right guaranteed in the
Charter
does not mean that the
Legislature had to anticipate such an occurrence and had to lay
down strict rules so such could not happen.

For these reasons I would dismiss the application but without
costs since neither the Board nor the Attorney-General are
asking for costs.

REID J. (dissenting):-- On its face, s. 28(1) of R.R.O. 1980,
Reg. 262 is mandatory. "A public school shall be opened ...
with religious exercises ..." [emphasis added]. A law that
requires the performance of religious exercises is a
restriction on freedom of religion. That is so even if the
exercise is of a person's own religion: see Dickson J. in R. v.
Big M Drug Mart Ltd.,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R. 295 at pp. 326-7, 18
D.L.R. (4th) 321 at pp. 346-7, [1985] 3 W.W.R. 481 at p. 510,
quoting Cartwright J. in Robertson and Rosetanni v. The Queen,

1963 CanLII 17 (SCC)
, [1963] S.C.R. 651, 41 D.L.R. (2d) 485, [1964] 1 C.C.C. 1.

Subsection (10) provides for an election. If standing
together, s-ss. (1) and (10) offer a truly free choice, there
would be no restriction, and nothing contrary to the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
. But do they?

Some applicants object simply to having to make a choice.
Others are non-religious, or members of non-Christian
religions. They do not wish their children to participate. But
they are reluctant to exercise their right to elect to have
their child excused from the exercises. This reluctance stems
from fear of the embarrassment, or the harm that might flow,
from having the child "singled out" and made to feel different
from his or her peers. As a result some feel compelled to
refrain from electing to have their child excused.

Both the purpose and the effect of the regulation are
relevant in determining constitutionality. If the purpose
violates the
Charter
, the regulation is invalid, and no inquiry
need be made into its effect: R. v. Big M, supra.

What is the purpose of s. 28? Is it to impose religious
exercises on public school children? Mr. Wright has displayed
to us the long history of concern on the part of the government
of Ontario and its advisers over the place of religious
instruction in the schools. Dr. Egerton Ryerson, the Chief
Superintendent of Education for Canada West (Ontario) between
1844 and 1876, is widely regarded as the founder of the public
school system. His "Report on A System of Public Elementary
Education for Upper Canada" (1846), favoured religious
instruction in the schools. His views were reflected in a
lecture he gave in 1847 to which Mr. Wright has drawn our
attention. Dr. Ryerson said:

I do not regard any instruction, discipline, or attainments,
as Education, which does not include Christianity ... "It is
the cultivation and exercise of man's moral powers and
feelings which forms the basis of social order and the vital
fluid of social happiness; and the cultivation of these is
the province of Christianity ..." See Hodgins, Documentary
History of Education in Upper Canada 1791 - 1876 Vol. VII, p.
148.

The Hope Commission (The Royal Commission on Education in
Ontario) was appointed by the Ontario government. It reported
in 1950. It shared Ryerson's view. At p. 36 of its report the
commission said:

Without proclaiming any creed or doctrine we know that in our
democracy the Christian ideals as personified and exemplified
by Jesus have an appeal to all persons of good will, and are
the surest common ground for an educational programme related
to the pupil as a person. The attitude of Jesus toward
children, His understanding of human nature and behaviour,
His charity and loving kindness toward all men, form a
perfect model for a true democracy in the classroom, the
community, and the nation.

The Mackay Report ("Religious Information and Moral
Development: The Report of the Committee on Religious Education
in the Public Schools of the Province of Ontario") was made in
1969. It reaffirmed that view. The report was prepared by a
committee appointed by the Ontario government, under the
chairmanship of the Honourable J. Keiller Mackay, a former
Lieutenant-Governor. In its preface, addressed to the
Honourable William G. Davis, Minister of Education for Ontario,
the committee said:

In accordance with our terms of reference, we have examined
and evaluated the present program; received representations
from all interested bodies; considered suggestions for
changes and improvement; studied means by which character,
ethics, social attitudes, and moral values and principles may
best be instilled in the young; considered the responsibility
of the public schools in these matters; and made
recommendations for your information and consideration.

At p. 35 of its report, the committee said:

It was also brought forcibly to the Committee's attention, as
previously noted, that to eliminate opening exercises would
suggest that religion is not an integral part of the life of
the people of this province. It is the Committee's view that
religion does indeed play a vital part in our life and that
the holding of opening exercises therefore exposes the child
to a valuable learning experience in relation to the whole
community in which he lives.

The Committee therefore recommends that opening exercises
consisting of the singing of the National Anthem and a
prayer, either of universal character appealing to God for
help in the day's activities, or the Lord's Prayer, be held
in the home rooms each morning in the elementary schools of
Ontario.

The uniformity of view expressed in these reports is
striking. From Egerton Ryerson in 1846 to the Mackay Committee
in 1969, every person, commission or committee appointed to
study the question and advise the Ontario government expressed
the same view; religious exercises are an essential component
of the public school curriculum.

The provision for an exemption, of one kind or other, has an
equally lengthy history. Thus, the School Act, 1843 (Can.), c.
29, provided that:

54. ... in the Common Schools or Town or City Schools
... no child shall be required to read or study in or from
any Religious Book, or to join in any exercise of Devotion or
Religion, which shall be objected to by his or her Parents or
Guardians.

There is thus a long history of opinion that religious
instruction and religious exercises are essential, or at the
least, highly desirable components of the public school
curriculum. Unless we assume that the governments of this
province ignored the recommendations repeatedly made to them,
we might reasonably conclude that s. 28(1) expresses a
conviction that religious exercises are desirable and should be
the rule or standard. That explains its mandatory tone. While
those who desire not to obey the rule may opt out, they must
perforce seek exceptional status.

There is a difference between imposing a rule in mandatory
terms and providing for exceptions, on the one hand, and
providing truly alternative choices on the other. Had the
object been to provide real freedom of choice, it could easily
have been achieved. All that was required was to provide that
there would be a time during the day when those who wished
could take part in religious exercises and those who did not,
need not. While such a provision might possibly have been
effected in some schools so as to make those who wished not to
participate feel "different" or "left out" in the hope that
they would join the participating group, the provision on its
face would not be objectionable under the
Charter
. But that is
not what was done, for that would not have achieved the result
that the commissions and committees uniformly thought should be
achieved.

On its face, therefore, the regulation discloses a purpose
contrary to the
Charter
: a purpose to interfere with religious
freedom.

Yet the inquiry need not stop there. Let us look at the
regulation's effect. About this we have evidence. Some
applicants feel compelled to refrain from asserting their right
to elect. Their feeling does not stem from fear of penal
sanctions of the type the courts were facing in Big M, R. v.
Videoflicks Ltd. et al. (1984),
1984 CanLII 44 (ON CA)
, 48 O.R. (2d) 395, 14 D.L.R.
(4th) 10, 15 C.C.C. (3d) 353, and Robertson. Yet is penal
sanction necessary to the existence of compulsion? May
compulsion not exist because of some lesser form of penalty? I
think it can. In Big M Dickson J. said at p. 336 S.C.R., p. 353
D.L.R., p. 517 W.W.R.:

A truly free society is one which can accommodate a wide
variety of beliefs, diversity of tastes and pursuits, customs
and codes of conduct.

At pp. 336-7 S.C.R., p. 354 D.L.R., p. 518 W.W.R., he said:

Coercion includes not only such blatant forms of compulsion
as direct commands to act or refrain from acting on pain of
sanction, coercion includes indirect forms of control which
determine or limit alternative courses of conduct available
to others.

(Emphasis added.) And again, loc. cit.:

What may appear good and true to a majoritarian religious
group, or to the state acting at their behest, may not, for
religious reasons, be imposed upon citizens who take a
contrary view. The
Charter
safeguards religious minorities
from the threat of "the tyranny of the majority".

I read these words to mean that compulsion may take many
forms. It may range from the direct, blatant, penal sanction to
lesser, indirect forms that nevertheless impose a limitation on
conduct. It may be that a control or limitation indirectly
imposed is not readily appreciable to those who are not
affected by it. It may be difficult for members of a
majoritarian religious group, as I am, to appreciate the
feelings of members of what, in our society, are minority
religions. It may be difficult for religious people to
appreciate the feelings of agnostics and atheists. Yet
nevertheless those feelings exist. No one has suggested that
the feelings expressed by applicants are not real, or that they
do not run deep.

Would anyone try? Is evidence needed to establish that some
parents might be so reluctant to stand on their rights they
will refrain? In the extreme case, if all of the pupils in the
class but one are Christians and willing to conform with the
rule, might not the sole Mohammedan, or Hebrew, or non-
believing child feel uncomfortable about the isolation
involved in opting out? Or, in a probably commoner case, if
most of the pupils willingly conform, might not a few whose
family faith is Moslem, or Hebraic or Buddhist, feel awkward
about seeking exemption? Peer pressures, and the desire to
conform, are notoriously effective with children. Does common
experience not tell us that these things are so, and that such
feelings might easily, and reasonably, lead some not to seek
exemption, and unwillingly conform, or others to seek it, and
be forced to suffer the consequences to their feelings and
convictions?

If that is so, some degree of coercion exists. In my view,
that would be difficult to deny. What the respondent, and the
Attorney-General, seem to say is: "Yes, some coercion does
exist, but those who feel it must put up with it, and so must
their children". That is said to be so because we are imperfect
creatures in an imperfect world and that perfect freedom cannot
exist. Thus, those who feel they cannot bring themselves to
request an exemption expect too much. They expect too much from
this Court, and from the
Charter
. Indeed, their difficulty
confers an advantage, for being singled out gives a child the
opportunity to build character by standing up to adversity.

The trouble with all of that, I say with respect, is that it
grants to the minority less freedom than the majority enjoy. If
every parent, or child, had to suffer adversity for the sake of
its beneficial effect on character, none could complain. But it
is not all of us who have to put up with it, or teach our
children to. It is only the objectors. The willing conformists
will not suffer, nor see their children suffer. To divide us
into two groups; those who have to put up with restriction of
their religious freedom and those who do not, is to deny the
freedom of religion that the
Charter
guarantees.

I cannot think how freedom can exist without equality in this
matter. The argument I am having trouble with appears to accept
some inequality, but says it is not much. But I think that
amounts to an Orwellian equality: some are more equal than
others. The complaint is made in this case by those who are
less equal.

I cannot accept the view that the objectors must pay a price
for their objection, when the willing conformists pay no price.
It does not seem to me to be the majority's function, or the
government of Ontario's function, to shake a finger at some
parents and say, you are too sensitive; you and your children
must pay a price for your beliefs; you should expose your
children to the embarrassment you fear because it is good for
them, and you and they must learn to wear your difference with
pride. If there were no reasonable basis for the feelings
expressed by applicants; if they were being silly, or
mischievous, their complaints should be ignored. But to me
their reactions are readily understandable. I cannot write them
off as merely contentious or fanciful. I accept them as real.

It is my profound conviction that the quality of freedom of
any society is measured by the way it treats its minorities.
This has always been so, but one need only look at pre-war
Germany, or present-day South Africa, where black people are a
political minority, to see that it is still so. It is thus
simply not acceptable for the majority to say, you minorities
cannot expect to enjoy the freedom we do because freedom cannot
be perfect when, for us, the majority in this matter, it is.
With respect, I consider that to be contrary to ethical
principle but, more importantly for this case, contrary to the

Charter
.

I must thus conclude that the effect of s. 28 is contrary to

s. 2(a)
and
s. 15
of the
Charter
.

Can it be saved by s. 1? Is it a reasonable limitation on
religious freedom? The criteria that must be satisfied were
laid down in R. v. Oakes,
1986 CanLII 46 (SCC)
, [1986] 1 S.C.R. 103, 26 D.L.R. (4th)
200, 65 N.R. 87. The first is that the governmental objective
sought to be advanced relates to concerns which are pressing
and substantial in a free and democratic society.

As I understand the argument, it is that morality is of
pressing concern, and that religious exercises are necessary to
its teaching. I have no doubt about the pressing need to
encourage morality, but that religious exercises are necessary
for its teaching is, in my opinion, a questionable proposition.
I accept that they may be helpful, but necessity I cannot
accept. I have, in my time, met dedicated non-religionists who
are nevertheless moral. But even accepting the proposition, is
the public school the proper instrument, or the necessary one?
Is it even the preferable one? What about the church (or
synagogue or mosque) and the home?

As to the uniformity of opinion expressed by the commissions
and committees preceding the regulation, and as to that forming
a basis for a governmental objective, I wonder if another were
appointed it would concur. A more recent opinion given by a
highly responsible body was to the contrary. Admittedly, it was
not appointed by the Ontario government. The opinion was that
of the Toronto Board of Education. The board adopted a
recommendation made to it by its Committee on Religious
Exercises and Religious Education in Elementary and Secondary
Schools that,

The Toronto Board of Education request the Minister of
Education to grant to this Board exemption from the teaching
of religious education in classrooms or schools of the Board;
and that the reason for this request be the multi-cultural
nature of our student population, as outlined in the Values
Education Report, which calls for an integration of a values
component in all areas of the curriculum.

That is an extract from the minutes of the Toronto Board of
Education of August 27, 1979. The board adopted a further
recommendation that the public schools within its jurisdiction
"be opened or closed each day with a prayer taking the form
of a minute's silent meditation".

The minutes of the board continue:

On August 23, 1979 (1979:785) the Board decided that each
school be opened or closed each school day with a prayer
taking the form of a minute's silent meditation, and not with
religious exercises consisting of the reading of the
Scriptures or other suitable readings and the repeating of
the Lord's Prayer or other suitable prayers, as required
under Ontario Regulation 704/78. The Board also decided to
request the Minister of Education to exempt the Board from
the teaching of religious education in the elementary
schools.

The Board considered a letter from the Minister of Education,
written in response to the above, advising that the Board's
decision to use the minute of silent meditation in place of
the Lord's Prayer or other suitable prayers is ultra vires
because it contravenes the requirements of Regulation 704/78.
The Minister granted the Board's request for exemption from
the teaching of religious education in the public schools.

The Board also considered a letter from William G. Davis,
Premier of Ontario, expressing his personal views with regard
to the Board's decision to substitute a minute of silent
meditation for the Lord's Prayer or other suitable prayers,
and urging the Board to reconsider its decision.

The Chairman of the Board recommended that the above
communication be received.

The board was thus prevented by the regulation from carrying
out its intention. Had the recommendation come from a body
appointed by the government of Ontario, I think it is
reasonable to consider that the result might have been
different. Was the board completely off base?

In my respectful opinion, no governmental concern has been
demonstrated so pressing as to justify the obvious interference
with religious freedom sought by and caused by the regulation.
Nor do I consider that the opinions of the bodies appointed by
the government to advise it in the past can reasonably be
accepted as binding upon it, and thus creating a pressing
necessity, or are even reflective of opinion today.

Finally, I do not think that s. 1 was intended to be applied
so as to justify an interference with the religious freedom of
some but not of others. That would make the
Charter
contradict
itself. If any interference may be justified by reason of s. 1,
it seems to me it must be an interference not with the right of
some to religious freedom, but with the right of all. In the
result, I do not think the regulation can be defended upon s.
1.

It has been submitted that the Sudbury Board should be given
an opportunity to modify its practice. The practice of the
Toronto Board of Education has been held up as an example. I
shall return to the story of the Toronto board, notwithstanding
that if the regulation is bad, the issue is irrelevant.

As a result of the Minister's objection, the board created a
volume entitled Readings & Prayers for use in Toronto Schools.
The board approved it in November, 1984, and claims copyright
in it. Its introductory passages reveal that it was intended
"to salute the multicultural diversity of Toronto" and to
deal with the demand imposed by s. 28(1). Although the
carefully worded ''introduction" mentions the board's 1979
resolution "that each school day under its jurisdiction be
opened or closed each day with a prayer taking the form of a
minute's silent meditation" it does not mention the Minister's
rejection of silent meditation as prayer.

It is a fascinating volume containing writings from the great
variety of religions practised in Toronto, from Baha'i-ism to
Zoroastrianism. Its legitimacy is not in issue before us. If it
were I would have serious doubts that it amounts to conformance
with s. 28(1). While much of it is clearly "prayer", and could
qualify as "other suitable prayer" within s. 28(1), and much is
easily recognized as "other suitable readings", some of it is
neither. The instructions for its use are:

Thus, opening or closing exercises in all Toronto schools are
as follows:

(a)  O Canada;

(b)  the reading of a minimum of one selection from the
Readings and Prayers;

(c)  suitable comment by the teachers or principal, if
necessary, concerning the origins of the selections used, as
indicated;

(d)  silent meditation.

My concern is three-fold. First, the reading of one selection
from "Readings and Prayers" would not be conformance with s.
28(1) which requires both readings and prayers, albeit one of
each would suffice. Secondly, there is no differentiation made
in the volume between prayers and readings; it gives no
guidance to any teacher who desires to conform with the letter
of s. 28(1).

Thirdly, and most importantly, many selections in the section
entitled "Readings and Prayers" do not pretend to be even
remotely religious. One entire subsection is of extracts from
the non-religious works of people whom the board regards as
adherents to "Secular Humanism". The board accepts that it is
questionable whether that is a religion at all. At p. 112 of
the volume, this occurs as part of a discussion of the
question:

Is secular humanism a religion? Many people, both humanist
and other, would argue that it is not. On the other hand,
both theists and humanists (such as Julian Huxley) take the
contrary position. Some theists may try to limit religion to
theism, a definition which eliminates some other important
Eastern religious traditions. It also fails to recognize the
element of faith in the secular world view. The faith is
different from that of the theist, but it is nevertheless
faith, and a number of humanists find no contradiction in
affiliating with bodies that call themselves religious. Some
humanists argue that what others believe is religion but what
they themselves believe is anti-religion. But it can be held
that their anti-religion is also a religious perspective.

The board leaves the question open, unless we are to take the
inclusion of this subsection as support for the view that anti-
religion is also religion. While that concept might be
acceptable to philosophers, I strongly doubt if the requirement
of "religious exercises" in s. 28(1) would be satisfied by
anti-religious exercises. In passing, I doubt if Shelley's
well-known poem "Ozymandias", included in this subsection at p.
130, has ever before been classified as a religious work.

The same might be said of Stevenson's "A Child's Garden of
Verses", from which the following is given as a suitable item.

The world is so full of a number of things  I'm sure we
should all be as happy as Kings.

"Other Readings" is a subsection of the "Readings and
Prayers" section. (Perhaps it is time to explain that while the
entire volume may be referred to briefly as Readings and
Prayers, it contains a section with that specific title.) The
board's instructions (at p. 12) state:

The Table of Contents indicates thirteen (13) sections, one
for each tradition, presented alphabetically starting with
Baha'i and concluding with Zoroastrianism. The thirteenth
section Other Readings, is not reserved for a tradition per
se, but under such headings as "thanksgiving", "beginning the
school day", "the seasons", ''love", "hope", "effort" and
"understanding", presents prayers and readings conveying
ideas and concepts that could be embraced by most religious
traditions.

The board thus places "Other Readings" in the same category
as selections under such headings as "Christianity" and
"Islam".

The subsection contains many selections that most people
would unhesitatingly recognize as religious, but it includes
also the following,

A seed of kindness to root  In lonely, meager soil,  In
growing strong its beauty called  To workmen in their toil,
And as the blossom petals fell  They left a cup of seeds ...

Enough to cheer a countryside  And all its people's needs.
If one small seed can do so much  Toward cheering up a few,
Just think of all the wondrous joy  The seeds of friendship
do.   (Mary O'Connor)

and Christina G. Rosetti's poem "Who Has Seen The Wind?"

Who has seen the wind?  Neither I nor you:  But when the
leaves hang trembling,  The wind is passing through.

Who has seen the wind?  Neither you nor I:  But when the
trees bow down their heads,  the wind is passing by.

No one could question the nobility of sentiment in the first,
and the poetic quality of the second of these poems has long
been accepted, but does a reading of either qualify as a
religious exercise?

Without disrespect to the Toronto board, whose sincere effort
has produced a work of scholarship and real value, I think it
has expanded the concept of other suitable readings and prayers
beyond the bounds of religious exercises, into non-religious
exercises. The requirement of s. 28(1) for religious exercises
is not satisfied by non-religious exercises. For that reason I
do not think that even if the Sudbury Board were to take the
pains and go to the lengths to which the Toronto Board has
gone, it could devise a practice that both conforms with s.
28(1) and meets the objections of the applicants.

In light of these views, it is not necessary for me to
examine the actual practice of the Sudbury Board. If s. 28(1)
is bad, as I believe it to be, the issue of practice is
irrelevant. If s. 28(1) is good, in my respectful opinion,
modification of Sudbury's practice to conform with Toronto's
would not amount to conformance with it.

There is thus no warrant for a discretionary withholding of
the remedy to which applicants are entitled. I would allow the
application.

ANDERSON J.:-- I have had the advantage of reading the
reasons for judgment given by O'Leary J. They set out
completely and with care the nature of the application and the
positions of the parties and I need not do so. I concur in his
disposition of the application and am not in disagreement with
his reasons. However, I would dispose of the case on bases
somewhat narrower, and for that reason, only, have chosen to
make some observations of my own.

Argument under
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter

The relevant portions of the
Canadian Charter of Rights and
Freedoms
are in the following terms:

Whereas Canada is founded upon principles that recognize
the supremacy of God and the rule of law:

. . . . .

2. Everyone has the following fundamental freedoms:

(a)  freedom of conscience and religion.

On this branch of the argument reference was made particularly
to three cases: R. v. Big M Drug Mart Ltd.,
1985 CanLII 69 (SCC)
, [1985] 1 S.C.R.
295, 18 D.L.R. (4th) 321, [1985] 3 W.W.R. 481 (S.C.C.); R. v.
Videoflicks Ltd. et al. (1984),
1984 CanLII 44 (ON CA)
, 48 O.R. (2d) 395, 14 D.L.R.
(4th) 10, 15 C.C.C. (3d) 353; Robertson and Rosetanni v. The
Queen,
1963 CanLII 17 (SCC)
, [1963] S.C.R. 651, 41 D.L.R. (2d) 485, [1964] 1 C.C.C. 1
(S.C.C.). Some preliminary examination of these cases is
appropriate before addressing the argument on this branch of
the case.

Big M Drug involved a constitutional challenge to the Lord's
Day Act, R.S.C. 1970, c. L-13. The case as heard in the Supreme
Court of Canada involved three constitutional questions. I am
concerned only with the first. Does the Lord's Day Act, and
especially s. 4 thereof, infringe upon the freedom of
conscience and religion guaranteed in
s. 2(a)
of the
Canadian
Charter of Rights and Freedoms
? The court unanimously answered
that question in the affirmative.

Dickson J., as he then was, under the caption of "Freedom of
religion" at pp. 336-7 S.C.R., pp. 353-4 D.L.R., pp. 517-8
W.W.R., has this to say:

A truly free society is one which can accommodate a wide
variety of beliefs, diversity of tastes and pursuits, customs
and codes of conduct. A free society is one which aims at
equality with respect to the enjoyment of fundamental
freedoms and I say this without any reliance upon
s. 15
of
the
Charter
. Freedom must surely be founded in respect for
the inherent dignity and the inviolable rights of the human
person. The essence of the concept of freedom of religion is
the right to entertain such religious beliefs as a person
chooses, the right to declare religious beliefs openly and
without fear of hindrance or reprisal, and the right to
manifest religious belief by worship and practice or by
teaching and dissemination. But the concept means more than
that.

Freedom can primarily be characterized by the absence of
coercion or constraint. If a person is compelled by the state
or the will of another to a course of action or inaction
which he would not otherwise have chosen, he is not acting of
his own volition and he cannot be said to be truly free. One
of the major purposes of the
Charter
is to protect, within
reason, from compulsion or restraint. Coercion includes not
only such blatant forms of compulsion as direct commands to
act or refrain from acting on pain of sanction, coercion
includes indirect forms of control which determine or limit
alternative courses of conduct available to others. Freedom
in a broad sense embraces both the absence of coercion and
constraint, and the right to manifest beliefs and practices.
Freedom means that, subject to such limitations as are
necessary to protect public safety, order, health, or morals
or the fundamental rights and freedoms of others, no one is
to be forced to act in a way contrary to his beliefs or his
conscience.

What may appear good and true to a majoritarian religious
group, or to the state acting at their behest, may not, for
religious reasons, be imposed upon citizens who take a
contrary view. The
Charter
safeguards religious minorities
from the threat of "the tyranny of the majority".

[At pp. 346-7 S.C.R., pp. 361-2 D.L.R., p. 526 W.W.R.]:

Viewed in this context, the purpose of freedom of
conscience and religion becomes clear. The values that
underlie our political and philosophic traditions demand that
every individual be free to hold and to manifest whatever
beliefs and opinions his or her conscience dictates, provided
inter alia only that such manifestations do not injure his or
her neighbour's or their parallel rights to hold and manifest
beliefs and opinions of their own. Religious belief and
practice are historically prototypical and, in many ways,
paradigmatic of conscientiously-held beliefs and
manifestations and are therefore protected by the
Charter
.
Equally protected, and for the same reasons, are expressions
and manifestations of religious non-belief and refusals to
participate in religious practice. It may perhaps be that
freedom of conscience and religion extends beyond these
principles to prohibit other sorts of governmental
involvement in matters having to do with religion. For the
present case it is sufficient in my opinion to say that
whatever else freedom of conscience and religion may mean, it
must at the very least mean this: government may not coerce
individuals to affirm a specific religious belief or to
manifest a specific religious practice for a sectarian
purpose.

(Emphasis added.) His conclusion on the constitutional question
posed above is found at p. 351 S.C.R., p. 365 D.L.R., p. 530
W.W.R., in the following terms:

In an earlier time, when people believed in the collective
responsibility of the community toward some deity, the
enforcement of religious conformity may have been a
legitimate object of government, but since the
Charter
, it is
no longer legitimate. With the Charter, it has become the
right of every Canadian to work out for himself or herself
what his or her religious obligations, if any, should be and
it is not for the state to dictate otherwise. The state shall
not use the criminal sanctions at its disposal to achieve a
religious purpose, namely, the uniform observance of the day
chosen by the Christian religion as its day of rest.

On the authorities and for the reasons outlined, the true
purpose of the Lord's Day Act is to compel the observance of
the Christian Sabbath and I find the Act, and especially s. 4
thereof, infringes upon the freedom conscience and religion
guaranteed in
s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
. The answer to the first
constitutional question will be in the affirmative.

[Emphasis added.]

Videoflicks was decided by the Court of Appeal before the
decision of the Supreme Court of Canada in Big M Drug Mart was
available. It concerned the validity of the Retail Business
Holidays Act, R.S.O. 1980, c. 453. The Act prohibited the
carrying on of certain retail business activities on holidays
as defined in the Act, including Sunday. Several accused
appealed convictions for carrying on a retail business or
offering goods or services for sale on a Sunday contrary to the
Act. Of the various businesses involved, one, Nortown Foods
Ltd., was owned by Orthodox Jews whose religion required them
to be closed on Saturday. The accused argued that the Act was
unconstitutional by reason of its infringement of the guarantee
of freedom of religion in
s. 2(a)
of the
Canadian Charter of
Rights and Freedoms
. The Court held that s. 2 of the Retail
Business Holidays Act was of no force and effect only as
concerned Nortown Foods Ltd. Under the caption "Freedom of
conscience and religion under the Charter", Tarnopolsky J.A.,
writing for the court, has this to say, at p. 420 O.R., p. 35
D.L.R.:

Freedom of conscience and religion under the
Charter

What follows is in no way to be taken as an exhaustive
definition of the fundamental freedom of religion embodied in

s. 2(a)
of the
Charter
. In my view, while it would certainly
include the rights enunciated by Ritchie J. in Robertson and
Rosetanni, supra, that definition is too restrictive. Freedom
of religion goes beyond the ability to hold certain beliefs
without coercion and restraint and entails more than the
ability to profess those beliefs openly. In my view, freedom
of religion also includes the right to observe the essential
practices demanded by the tenets of one's religion and, in
determining what those essential practices are in any given
case, the analysis must proceed not from the majority's
perspective of the concept of religion but in terms of the
role that the practices and beliefs assume in the religion of
the individual or group concerned.

In the disposition of the case, the following appears at p. 430
O.R., p. 45 D.L.R.:

In accordance with
s. 52(1)
of the
Constitution Act, 1982
,
